title: Wall Street Strategists Call Stock Rout a Fresh Reason to Buy
detail:
Wall Street Strategists Call Stock Rout a Fresh Reason to Buy
Bloomberg · Bloomberg
Emily Forgash
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 7:30 AM CST 4 min read
^GSPC
^NDX

(Bloomberg) -- A slew of Wall Street strategists were banking on a short-term selloff following the US midterm elections to give investors an opportunity to buy stocks at a discount.

Most Read from Bloomberg

Rubio Weighs Leaving Administration After GOP's Midterm Loss

Hinojosa Seeks 'Balance' With Musk, Regulations in Blue Texas

Microsoft Winding Down Oracle Deal to Rent AI Cloud Capacity

Morgan Stanley Offers $2.3 Billion Debt for Dell Family Deal

Sony Debuts $60 Wired Headphones With '80s-Inspired Design

On Thursday, they got far more than they bargained for. And now they're urging their clients to take advantage.

"This is the place where you should be adding risk over the next two to three weeks," said Mike Wilson, chief US equity strategist at Morgan Stanley.

Wilson was just as surprised as everyone else at the severity of the selling on Thursday that sent the S&P 500 Index down 4.4% and the Nasdaq 100 Index tumbling 6.4% due to concerns that newly empowered Democrats will slow the artificial intelligence build out.

Still, Wilson is confident that US stocks are poised for a rally, and he's sticking to his target for the S&P 500 to reach 8,000 by the end of the year, which would imply a gain of 8.4% from Friday's close.

Investors waded back into the market on Friday, sending the S&P 500 up 0.3%. But the benchmark is still down 2.5% since polls closed on Tuesday. Democrats won control of the Senate and House of Representatives, as well as numerous state houses and governor's mansions throughout the country. Many of the winning candidates pledged to check data center development and increase regulation.

The wipeout is evidence that the selloff in the S&P 500 in recent weeks is nearing an end, not a sign that the AI trade is collapsing, which would signal more pain ahead, Wilson and many of his Wall Street colleagues argue.

"We have had an AI bubble and I think the air is coming out of that bubble," Ed Yardeni, chief investment strategist at Yardeni Research, said in an interview on Thursday. "Bursting would mean that it would have significant adverse impacts on the economy, and I don't see that happening."

Wilson is recommending investors scoop up shares of consumer-focused stocks, particularly if interest rates and oil prices keep falling, while Yardeni likes healthcare stocks.

"I view it as a correction," said Yardeni, who has a year-end S&P 500 target of 7,900. "I anticipated buying opportunities after the elections, and I think we're starting to see some pretty good ones."

DoorDash Rose 13% in a Week. Is the $17 Billion Instacart Deal Really That Good? ©@ckstockphoto via Canva
Key Takeaways

DoorDash (DASH) stock gained 13% from October 26 to November 2, outperforming the Nasdaq 100 ETF's roughly 4% decline after record quarterly earnings and a major acquisition announcement.

Instacart (CART) agreed to be acquired for approximately $17 billion, bringing DoorDash grocery delivery capabilities and a valuable advertising business.

Uber (UBER) reportedly explored acquiring Instacart, while Consumer Edge data showed DoorDash accounted for 59% of tracked delivery-app spending, compared with 18% for Uber Eats.

DoorDash's earnings growth supports the deal, but its cash-heavy financing, regulatory uncertainty, and integration costs make the acquisition's long-term returns critical.

DoorDash (DASH) stock climbed approximately 13% from October 26 to November 2 after the company reported record third-quarter earnings and announced plans to acquire Instacart (CART) for approximately $17 billion.

The transaction could strengthen DoorDash's grocery delivery operations while intensifying competition with Uber (UBER), which reportedly held preliminary acquisition discussions with Instacart.

Although DoorDash's underlying business continues to grow, the acquisition introduces financing and regulatory risks that could affect shareholder returns.

What Happened?

DoorDash reported record third-quarter results on October 29, with marketplace gross order value increasing 36% to $33.9 billion and revenue rising 34% to $4.6 billion.

Excluding Deliveroo, revenue increased 23% year over year, showing that DoorDash's existing operations continued growing independently of its recent acquisition.

Net income jumped 91% to $466 million, representing diluted earnings of approximately $1.06 per share, compared with analysts' expectations of $0.81.

The company also announced its agreement to acquire Instacart for $65 per share, representing a 26% premium to Instacart's October 22 closing price.

At least 75% of the transaction consideration will be paid in cash, while DoorDash stock is capped at 25%.

Instacart generated approximately $3.75 billion in revenue during 2025, including $1.07 billion from advertising and other services, representing roughly 28% of total revenue.

In the acquisition announcement, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said, "Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online," highlighting why Instacart's established technology and retail relationships could strengthen the combined business.

The competitive implications are significant.

According to Consumer Edge data cited in TIKR's DoorDash acquisition analysis, DoorDash represented approximately 59% of tracked delivery-app spending in the third quarter, while Instacart and Uber Eats each accounted for 18%.

The broader market moved higher Friday, recovering some of Thursday's rout as dip buying in chipmakers and AI-infrastructure stocks lifted the broader market. Weakness in software stocks on Friday limited overall market upside and kept the Dow Jones Industrials in negative territory.

Stocks also found support Friday on better-than-expected US economic news. The Oct nonfarm payrolls and average hourly earnings rose more than expected, and the unemployment rate unexpectedly declined. Consumer sentiment also improved, and inflation expectations declined in the University of Michigan's Nov consumer sentiment index.

US Oct nonfarm payrolls rose by +165,000, stronger than expectations of +70,000 and the biggest increase in 7 months. Also, Sep nonfarm payrolls were revised upward to +60,000 from the previously reported +29,000. The Oct unemployment rate unexpectedly fell -0.1 to 4.1% versus expectations of no change at 4.2%.

US Oct average hourly earnings rose +0.4% m/m and +3.1% y/y, stronger than expectations of +0.3% m/m and +2.9% y/y.

The University of Michigan US Nov consumer sentiment index rose +3.0 to 51.0, stronger than expectations of no change at 48.0.

The University of Michigan US Nov 1-year inflation expectations fell -0.4 to 4.3%, weaker than expectations of 4.6%. The Nov 5-10 year inflation expectations fell -0.1 to 3.4%, weaker than expectations of no change at 3.5%.

Hawkish Fed comments on Friday were negative for stocks and bonds. New York Fed President Williams said that inflation is "absolutely too high" and monetary policy "does have a critical role in making sure that these relative price shocks don't translate into broader or more persistent inflation." Also, San Francisco Fed President May Daly said inflation has been high for too long and "My expectation is we're going to have to tighten monetary policy further," but it is still too soon to know how much higher rates will need to go.

title: Q4 QQQ Roadmap: Navigating AI Turbulence & Market Headwinds

Q4 QQQ Roadmap: Navigating AI Turbulence & Market Headwinds

Let's look at what's actually happening with the Nasdaq 100 (QQQ) as we wrap up 2026.

If you step back and look at the big picture, three clear takeaways stand out:

1) The market is still climbing a massive wall of worry. If someone had told you earlier this year where oil prices and interest rates would end up, you probably wouldn't have believed the market could hold up this well. 

2) AI is carrying the entire narrative. Right now, the economy and the stock market are practically glued to AI. The moment investors worry that data center or infrastructure spending might slow down, tech stocks take an immediate hit.

3) The broad indices don't tell the full story. Serious rotation is happening under the hood. 

From Market Savior to "Tech Destruction" 

Remember last year when everyone complained that big tech was single-handedly dragging the rest of the market up? The script has flipped. QQQ just logged its worst three-day drop since "Liberation Day." In fact, Morgan Stanley noted that U.S. tech momentum recently hit levels worse than during the dot-com bust.

So, what's holding equities back right now? It boils down to four main worries:

• Inflation and stubborn interest rates

• Political headwinds surrounding AI

• Debt and funding fears in AI infrastructure

• Pure technical gravity and profit-taking

Here is why there's good reason to believe the market will push past these hurdles in the coming months.

Inflation & Interest Rates

Recent energy spikes reignited inflation fears and pushed yields higher, but geopolitical energy shocks are usually short-lived. We've already seen oil cool off following reports of potential progress on a U.S.–Iran agreement.

On the rate front, market projections lean toward 3 to 4 quarter-point hikes extending into mid-to-late 2027. But as the team at BlueKurtic Market Insights pointed out, stocks can actually perform quite well during rate-hiking cycles—provided the pace is steady.

This looks more like a limited, non-cyclical adjustment (likely capping out at 2 to 3 hikes) rather than an aggressive tightening regime. The last time we saw a similar non-cyclical adjustment was in 1997, and the S&P 500 went on to gain 40% over the following year.

Politics & the Midterm Effect: Why Gridlock is Good

AI buildouts have run into public pushback—a recent Reuters poll showed only about a third of Americans approve of the current rapid pace of data-center construction. Markets have also been trying to price in the political "Blue Wave," which added fuel to the tech sell-off over fears of tighter regulation.

However, markets are forward-looking mechanisms. This setup is shaping up to be a classic "sell the rumor, buy the news" event.

Historically, a divided government is actually great for stocks—divided setups typically deliver higher average returns than when one party controls both Congress and the White House. On top of that, midterm seasonality is heavily on our side: the S&P 500 has finished higher six months after every single midterm election since 1950. That's 19 straight elections with an average gain of nearly 15%, regardless of who won.

AI Debt & Funding Fears

Fears spiked in October when CoreWeave (CRWV) saw its bond yields jump to distressed levels, causing its stock to tumble. The market briefly priced CRWV as if bankruptcy were imminent—at one point in September, Polymarket showed a 50% chance of a 2027 bankruptcy.

Today? That probability has plummeted to just 12%. The extreme solvency fears were largely overblown.

Technical Gravity & Necessary Reset 

Earlier this year, several AI stocks simply went too far, too fast.

Take SanDisk (SNDK): it blew way past its Fibonacci extensions, surged 4,000% in a single year, and stretched 264% above its 200-day moving average. Anything more than 200% above that trendline is extreme. Think of the 200-day moving average as a rubber band—stretch it too far, and it inevitably snaps back.

Even the strongest market leaders need to reset. What we're seeing right now across names like Marvell (MRVL), Arm Holdings (ARM), and Micron (MU) is a standard pullback to test those major moving averages. Historically, that first test of a rising 200-day line offers one of the best risk-reward entry points you can ask for. 

Bottom Line 

While scary headlines around AI leverage, rates, and politics caused a sharp pull-back, the underlying technical frame of this market remains healthy. Extended tech leaders are flushing out excess leverage and returning to key support levels. Combined with favorable post-midterm seasonality and the benefits of political gridlock, this reset looks less like the end of the run and more like a setup for the next leg higher.

Stock Futures Mixed After Bruising Thursday Session

Stock futures point to a mixed opening—and a potential shift in momentum after yesterday's big retreat. Futures tied to the Nasdaq 100 were up about 1.4% after the tech-heavy index entered correction territory on Thursday. Futures tied to the S&P 500 were up about 0.2% the morning after it dropped 4.4%. The Dow appeared poised to extend yesterday's losses, with futures tied to the blue-chip index down some 0.9%.

Bitcoin prices slumped more than 5% over the past 24 hours, with the digital currency recently trading around $76,000. Precious metals, including gold, were falling, with a troy ounce of gold selling for about $4,081. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield ticked up slightly to 4.86%. Oil prices were also rising: West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was up about 0.6% to about $90.06 a barrel, while Brent crude, the global benchmark, was up 0.4% to $98.66.

Will Tech Stocks Bounce Today?

AI-related stocks that were among the market's worst performers on Thursday may manage to recover today. Data center company Iren (IREN) was among the top premarket climbers, jumping more than 15%. SanDisk (SNDK) was recently up more than 10% while Western Digital (WDC), Micron Technology (MU), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Seagate Technology (STX) were also rising. The Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) was recently up almost 7%, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was up more than 5%.

Elon Musk's two public companies were also rising, with SpaceX (SPCX) up about 5% and Tesla (TSLA) nearly 2%. Musk in an early morning tweet reaffirmed his commitment to Tesla's evolution, saying it would wind down Cybertruck production next year to open factory space for Cybercabs.

Tech sector sentiment is also getting a boost from strong results posted by Cloudflare (NET), another AI investor favorite. Shares of the networking and security services provider, which reported after yesterday's closing bell, were up nearly 20% in premarket trading. Shares of Airbnb (ABNB) jumped 14% after the short-term property rental marketplace boosted its guidance.

title: Stock Indexes Push Higher as Chipmakers Roar Back
detail:
Stock Indexes Push Higher as Chipmakers Roar Back
Rich Asplund
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 10:18 AM CST 8 min read
^GSPC
^DJI
^IXIC
^NDX

The S&P 500 Index ($SPX) (SPY) is up +1.07% today, the Dow Jones Industrial Average ($DOWI) (DIA) is up +0.21%, and the Nasdaq 100 Index ($IUXX) (QQQ) is up +2.09%. December E-mini S&P futures (ESZ26) are up +0.90%, and December E-mini Nasdaq futures (NQZ26) are up +2.00%.

US stock indices are moving higher today, with the Dow Jones Industrials recovering from a 4-week low. The broader market is mostly higher today, recovering some of Thursday's rout as dip buying in chipmakers and AI-infrastructure stocks lifts the broader market. Stocks plummeted on Thursday amid speculation that the Democratic sweep of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections will usher in a new era of regulation for the artificial-intelligence industry. The rotation out of chipmakers reflects a growing view that public opposition to data centers could crimp the growth of chipmakers and data-center suppliers. The weakness in software stocks today is limiting the upside in the overall market.

Stocks added to their gains today on better-than-expected US economic news. The Oct nonfarm payrolls and average hourly earnings rose more than expected, and the unemployment rate unexpectedly declined. Consumer sentiment also improved, and inflation expectations declined in the University of Michigan's Nov consumer sentiment index.

US Oct nonfarm payrolls rose by +165,000, stronger than expectations of +70,000 and the biggest increase in 7 months. Also, Sep nonfarm payrolls were revised upward to +60,000 from the previously reported +29,000. The Oct unemployment rate unexpectedly fell -0.1 to 4.1% versus expectations of no change at 4.2%.

US Oct average hourly earnings rose +0.4% m/m and +3.1% y/y, stronger than expectations of +0.3% m/m and +2.9% y/y.

The University of Michigan US Nov consumer sentiment index rose +3.0 to 51.0, stronger than expectations of no change at 48.0.

The University of Michigan US Nov 1-year inflation expectations fell -0.4 to 4.3%, weaker than expectations of 4.6%. The Nov 5-10 year inflation expectations fell -0.1 to 3.4%, weaker than expectations of no change at 3.5%.

Hawkish comments today from New York Fed President Williams were negative for stocks and bonds as he said that inflation is "absolutely too high" and monetary policy "does have a critical role in making sure that these relative price shocks don't translate into broader or more persistent inflation."
